articles.title: Trump adds extra sanctions to Russian bank for ties to Iran
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Monday added extra sanctions on one of Russia’s largest financial institutions, VTB, over its ties to Iran, layering on penalties first imposed because of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Treasury Department is redesignating VTB as part of the administration’s “Operation Economic Outcast.” The sanctions campaign was launched in August to…
articles.body:
The Trump administration on Monday added extra sanctions on one of Russia’s largest financial institutions, VTB, over its ties to Iran, layering on penalties first imposed because of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Treasury Department is redesignating VTB as part of the administration’s “Operation Economic Outcast.” The sanctions campaign was launched in August to squeeze Iran financially as the Islamic Republic has resisted more than six months of U.S. military bombardment and effectively held the world’s energy supply hostage through its military threats on the Strait of Hormuz .

Iran’s support for the Houthis in Yemen, who have recently taken over critical infrastructure on the Red Sea, has recently threatened another key energy maritime route.

“Under Operation Economic Outcast, Treasury will continue to target and disrupt those who provide material, technological, or financial support that allows the Iranian regime to sustain its terrorist enterprise,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent.

“Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran’s enablers.”

VTB is Russia’s second largest financial institution with thousands of branches across the world, particularly across India, southeast Asia and China. The Biden administration first designated the bank in 2022 following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Trump administration’s new sanctions are an effort to encourage countries and institutions to cut ties with VTB by publicizing its role helping Iran evade sanctions and finance its international terrorism activity.

This includes VTB helping Iran move billions of dollars in frozen assets and enabling tens of millions of dollars in transactions for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Force (IRGC), the military force primarily responsible for Iran’s terrorist activity across the world.

State Department spokesperson Tommy Piggott said today’s actions “sends a clear message to governments and financial institutions considering similar arrangements: any effort to help Iran evade sanctions will carry serious consequences, including exposure to U.S. financial restrictions.”

Still, it’s not entirely clear the main impact of the additional sanctions. Treasury officials will meet with international financial institutions this week to provide them information to shut down revenue streams and procurement networks tied to the Iranian regime, the IRGC, Iran’s terrorist proxies and other beneficiaries, The Hill has learned.

The sanctions prevent any U.S. person or entity from doing business with VTB and prohibits transactions with any entities with a 50 percent or more ownership by the blocked entity.

articles.title: Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran tour following Palestine advocacy
articles.summary: Gillette Stadium owner cites concerns over Macklemore’s rhetoric as reason for barring him from performances.
articles.body:
Billionaire Robert Kraft has confirmed that Macklemore has been barred from Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, after the rapper said his support for Palestine led to his being dropped from pop star Ed Sheeran’s tour.

Kraft said in a statement received by Al Jazeera on Monday that Macklemore’s recent performances and what he described as a “broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery” led Gillette Stadium, which is owned and operated by the Kraft group, to determine that his appearances there on September 25 and 26 “would cross that line”.

“This decision is not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf,” Kraft said. “But that advocacy should not come at the expense of the Jewish community or obscure the responsibility of Hamas … whose horrific actions have caused immeasurable suffering for Palestinians and Israelis alike.”

Kraft’s statement came after Macklemore claimed Sheeran informed him that Kraft was barring him from performing at Gillette Stadium. Macklemore also alleged that Kraft had rallied other stadium owners to issue an ultimatum: “If Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues.”

Kraft did not directly address the claim that he had contacted other stadium owners.

Macklemore made the allegations in a lengthy Instagram statement on Monday, the same day promoter Messina Touring Group confirmed that venues had refused to host upcoming shows with the rapper on the lineup.

“I’m not sure how to start this. So I’m going to speak from the heart and share the truth,” Macklemore wrote. “Ed Sheeran and his team have made the decision to remove me from The Loop tour.”

But Macklemore said neither he nor Sheeran, nor singer Pink, who had reposted criticism of his performance, were the victims in the controversy.

Messina Touring Group, the tour promoter, confirmed Macklemore’s removal from the tour in a statement to Rolling Stone magazine on Monday⁠.

“We have been notified by venues on the upcoming US tour dates that they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans,” the Messina Touring Group said. “After discussions with stakeholders, Macklemore will not be performing on the remaining support dates.”

Al Jazeera has not independently verified Macklemore’s account, and neither Sheeran nor his press office has commented.

Macklemore described Sheeran as a close friend of 13 years and said the two had several difficult conversations over the past week.

“He couldn’t get past his public-facing, ‘I don’t take sides,’” Macklemore wrote, referring to Sheeran’s reluctance to take a public stance on Israel’s war on Gaza.

The controversy began after Macklemore’s performances at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on September 4 and 5, where he repeatedly voiced support for Palestinians and performed Hind’s Hall , his protest song inspired by the pro-Palestinian student movement.

The Israeli American Council later launched a petition calling for Macklemore to be removed from Sheeran’s tour. Pink also reposted criticism of the performance that called for an apology and ticket refunds.

Macklemore argued that performing alongside one of the world’s biggest artists had made his advocacy more threatening to those who opposed it.

“If I kept doing the shows, saying Free Palestine, with Ed implicitly supporting it, the crowd getting loud and showing undeniable support for Palestinian liberation, what artist might speak out next?” he wrote.

He said he hoped the dispute would not end his friendship with Sheeran, but made clear he did not regret speaking out.

articles.title: Inside the Houthis’ expanding war economy in Yemen
articles.summary: The Houthis have restructured Yemen’s commercial sector, securing billions in revenue amid a humanitarian crisis.
articles.body:
The Houthi rebels in Yemen have control of the Red Sea coast, including the major port city of Hodeidah, and have developed a centralised financial system generating approximately $2.5bn annually through taxes, customs duties, and other levies.

The Houthis have reshaped the private sector in areas under their control, focusing on sectors that offer the greatest potential for revenue collection and control, such as general trade, imports, and food commodities.

The US government alleges that the Houthis generate over $2bn annually through illicit oil sales, with Iran providing oil to the group through complex financial networks, including cryptocurrency transactions and local exchange houses, despite extensive international sanctions.

The rapid advance by Yemen's Houthis down the country's Red Sea coast has raised questions over whether the group could turn its territorial gains into new sources of revenue, adding to an already extensive war economy.

But the Houthis already had control of large sections of the Red Sea coast, including the major port city of Hodeidah, and the financial benefits associated with that. Their military gains over the past week do not necessarily change the restrictions they have to deal with as an internationally unrecognised governing authority.

Ahmed al-Shalafi, Al Jazeera's Yemeni affairs editor, said that the advance has been a "geographical and military gain" but not an economic one, as it doesn't remove the international sanctions that have been placed on it, which severely restrict their ability to commercially exploit the new territory under its control through formal international channels.

But the Houthis already enjoy significant financial benefits from their long-time control of northwestern Yemen, the most populous part of the country.

Since the Houthis' capture of the capital Sanaa in September 2014, the group has developed a centralised financial system to collect revenues through taxes, customs duties, zakat (religious alms), and other levies.

A July report by the Mokha Center for Strategic Studies described this as a "parallel economy", estimating that the system generated direct and indirect financial resources and costs worth approximately $2.5bn annually.

Of that total, the report estimated that around $800m came from taxes and customs, $600m from additional feeds and levies, and $300m from cash and in-kind contributions to the war effort. It also counted about $100m linked to mobilisation events and another $700m in indirect costs borne by businesses through higher transport, service, and fee-related expenses.

The Houthi authorities have also revoked the licenses of 4,225 established commercial agencies – the legal local representatives for foreign companies – according to a July report by Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies, which said the move could pave the way for businesses affiliated with the group to take their place. For their part, the Houthis defended the move, claiming that the agencies had not renewed their registrations for three years.

But Houssam al-Saeedi, an economic researcher and the head of the Economic Studies Program at the Yemen and Gulf Center for Studies, told Al Jazeera that he viewed the restructuring as deliberate.

"It seizes companies belonging to existing merchants and manages them in favour of the [Houthis]," al-Saeedi noted. "What is happening is a network aimed primarily at bringing about a change or replacement of capital; so that even in the event of reaching a political settlement or a military victory, this group retains financial sources in the future."

The Houthis reject the characterisation of their economic policies as simply an effort to tighten control over the private sector, saying measures introduced in recent years are intended to encourage domestic production, investment and small businesses, and simplify commercial regulation.

Houthi commercial activity has increasingly shifted towards sectors that offer the greatest potential for revenue collection and control.

The Mokha Center data showed that 26 percent of the nearly 68,000 commercial records analysed by the study were in general trade and imports, followed by food commodities at 18 percent.

"The Houthi group established a completely separate system, based on creating an internal economy parallel to the actual available economy first," al-Saeedi explained to Al Jazeera.

He said the group uses state mechanisms to collect official taxes while simultaneously extracting non-state levies.

"There are various, long, and large collection operations under the name of 'supporting the war effort' and others, and these are not taken through government mechanisms."

Beyond revenues raised inside Yemen, the US government says illicit oil trading has become one of the Houthis' most important sources of external financing.

The US Treasury Department alleged in January that the Houthis generate more than $2bn annually through illicit oil sales. It said Iran sells and provides oil to the group, including free monthly shipments, using Iranian-owned or affiliated companies based in Dubai.

Al-Saeedi said that the group has long prioritised the energy sector.

"These companies work primarily as a front for money laundering for the group," he stated, adding that smuggled oil could provide direct income through domestic sales and monopoly pricing.

Al-Saeedi said that the Houthis used a range of illicit channels to move weapons, oil, and money, including smuggling networks and financial laundering. Another source of Houthi financing, he said, came from Iranian oil sold to third parties, with the proceeds transferred to the group through complex financial networks, including cryptocurrency transactions and local exchange houses.

The networks operate under extensive international sanctions. The US designates the Houthis as both a "Foreign Terrorist Organisation" and a "Specially Designated Global Terrorist" group. The United Nations Security Council separately lists the Houthis under its Yemen sanctions regime, subjecting the group to a targeted arms embargo.

"Cutting off external funding to the Houthis may lead to suffocating them, but they have other sources of income, of course," al-Shalafi said.

The Houthis have previously denied using Iranian fuel to finance their operations.

The Houthis' extensive revenue-raising network exists alongside a deepening economic and humanitarian crisis in the areas it controls and across Yemen more broadly.

The UN estimated in March that 22.3 million people in Yemen require humanitarian assistance and protection.

In Houthi-controlled areas the crisis is compounded by the fact that public sector employees have not received salary payments for years. The economic misery has led to increasing public criticism of the Houthis in the areas under their control, despite the group's intolerance for dissent.

Al-Shalafi pointed out that the group's regional actions are deeply tied to this domestic reality, seeking an escape from crises over unpaid salaries and high prices.

"They transformed these economic crises into a combat priority, turning them into war, confrontation, and mobilisation," al-Shalafi said. "The war, of course, gives them the justification to continue imposing levies, for military spending, and to postpone the entitlements of the people inside."

The Houthis say the root cause of the issue – the lack of payment of public sector salaries – stems from the transfer of the headquarters of the Central Bank of Yemen to government-controlled Aden, and the loss of access to the country's oil and gas revenues. They accuse Saudi Arabia, which backs the Yemeni government, of blockading them.

Can the Houthis profit from their gains?

The question now is whether control of the coastline, ports, and territory around the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern entrance to the Red Sea, will substantially expand the group's financial power – or primarily increase its military leverage.

"[Houthi] control over the Mocha coast and Bab al-Mandab will not be met by a world standing idly by or paying royalties and levies to the Houthis; there will be a confrontation or conflict of some kind to settle this issue," al-Shalafi said.

Whatever the effect of the latest territorial gains, Yemen already has two increasingly separate economic systems, posing long-term challenges.

"There are two completely different economies in the Houthi-controlled areas and the government-controlled areas," al-Sa'eedi said. "In my view, these current economic complexities cannot be resolved without a decisive military outcome that controls the ground, or a comprehensive political settlement."

articles.title: US scraps limits on emissions from coal and gas power plants
articles.summary: The Environment Protection Agency says the move will save the country billions of dollars and reduce energy prices.
articles.body:
Rules aimed at limiting pollution from coal and gas power plants are being scrapped, the head of the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has announced.

The agency also said it would take steps to prevent future administrations from regulating power plant emissions.

The EPA said that getting rid of the majority of the climate rules from President Joe Biden's era would save $310bn (£223bn) and reduce energy prices.

But environmental groups warned it would come at a huge cost to Americans' health and the planet. The EPA's move is expected to face immediate legal challenges.

"The reality is that America produces energy better and cleaner than anywhere else in the world, and our power plants should not be unfairly targeted," the head of the EPA, Lee Zeldin, said on Monday.

Fossil fuels, which include coal and natural gas, are by far the largest driver of global climate change, according to the United Nations.

The EPA said in a statement that it found the Biden-era rules on power plant emissions had "exceeded the agency's authority".

The agency said the regulations required "control technologies that are not adequately demonstrated, effectively forcing plants to retire rather than setting standards they could actually meet".

The EPA is also seeking to get rid of all other greenhouse gas rules for the power sector.

The changes, which will undergo public scrutiny, were proposed last year by Zeldin.

He said the new rules would "ensure affordable and reliable energy supplies and drive down the costs of transportation, heating, utilities, farming, and manufacturing while boosting our national security".

The Biden-era regulations called for a major reduction in carbon emissions from power plants, as well as vehicles and industrial facilities. It was estimated that the measures would stop 4,500 premature deaths annually.

But the EPA said on Monday: "Any potential public health harms are too uncertain, conjectural, remote, and convoluted to tie specifically to the US power sector."

Zeldin told reporters that safeguards against "hazardous air pollutants" would remain in place "to safeguard human health".

Nathaniel Keohane, president of the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions – an independent environmental organisation – described the move as "a giant step backward".

"In repealing carbon pollution standards for power plants, EPA has ignored sound science and economics and abdicated its responsibility to protect public health and welfare," Keohane added.

The US is currently the second-biggest emitter of planet-warming greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide, behind China.

And the power sector makes up about a quarter of US emissions, at roughly 1.5 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent each year, according to the latest available estimates.

That means the US power sector emissions are higher than the total emissions of all but a handful of countries.

US power sector emissions have been generally falling over the past couple of decades, albeit with a slight uptick last year, as coal use has fallen.

But Trump has long argued for a resurgence in coal power and has regularly criticised renewables such as wind and solar.

The precise consequences of today's announcement for US emissions - and global climate change - are uncertain.

Some researchers question whether coal will ever make the resurgence that Trump hopes for. They point to the sharp falls in costs of many clean technologies such as solar power over the past decade.

In 2022, the EPA lost some of its powers to limit greenhouse gas emissions when the Supreme Court ruled in favour of 19 states and some of the nation's largest coal companies, which were worried about the economic cost of the policy and argued the agency did not have the authority to limit emissions across whole states.

Monday's announcement is the latest move by President Donald Trump's administration to walk back policies designed to combat global warming and climate change.

In February, the EPA reversed a landmark Obama-era scientific ruling, which held that greenhouse gases were a threat to public health. This was challenged by several states and local governments.

articles.title: ED arrests ex-OSD of Baghel for role in Chhattisgarh job scam
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Enforcement Directorate (ED) on Monday said it has arrested former Chhattisgarh CM Bhupesh Baghel's former OSD Chetan Borghariya, who is pr.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Enforcement Directorate (ED) on Monday said it has arrested former Chhattisgarh CM Bhupesh Baghel's former OSD Chetan Borghariya, who is presently additional collector of Balrampur-Ramanujganj, in the case of illegal appointments of DSPs and collectors through exam paper leaks.ED, which had earlier arrested former state public service commission (PSC) chief Taman Singh Sonwani, claimed it has traced the alleged proceeds of crime linked to bank accounts of Borghariya and other officials.Borghariya, who was arrested on Sept 11, has been remanded in six-day ED custody by a special PMLA court in Raipur. The agency is probing alleged money laundering relating to irregularities and manipulation in the CGPSC State Service Examinations, 2020 and 2021."Investigation revealed that other accused, Utkarsh Chandrakar, Anil Chandrakar and Dr Vikash Chandrakar, allegedly collected illegal gratification exceeding Rs 3 crore from various candidates of 2021 CGPSC examination, on assurance of providing them question papers in advance and securing their selection by using their purported access and influence in the then CM's office," ED said.The probe further revealed that the name and official position of Chetan Borghariya, who was then posted as OSD in CM's office, was allegedly used in connection with such assurances."The evidence gathered during probe, including digital evidence, banking transactions and recorded statements, revealed involvement of Borghariya in processes and activities connected with the proceeds of crime, including their acquisition, possession, concealment and use," ED alleged.According to the agency, the leaked question papers were provided to certain candidates prior to the examinations. "Candidates assembled at Siddhi Vinayak Marriage Palace, Raipur, prior to the preliminary examination, where the leaked question paper was allegedly distributed to them. Subsequently, candidates were accommodated at Barnawapara Sanctuary Resort, where coaching was allegedly imparted based on leaked papers relating to the mains examination," ED said.ED claimed it has seized evidence related to cash deposits of Rs 66.64 lakh through 170 transactions in the bank account of Borghariya during the relevant period. Multiple financial transactions between Borghariya and Utkarsh have also been detected.Searches were conducted on premises of Borghariya on Sept 1, with digital devices, including mobile phones, being seized. "Investigation has also revealed financial transactions involving Figurecave E-Com (OPC) Pvt Ltd, which is suspected to have been used for the layering and movement of funds," ED claimed.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed dismisses questions about Hasan Piker ties on 'Face the Nation,' pivots to groceries
articles.summary: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed deflected questions about Hasan Piker on "Face the Nation," pivoting to grocery prices.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed rejected questions on Sunday regarding his relationship with Hasan Piker, saying that the race was not about "a Twitch streamer in California." CBS News' Weijia Jiang asked El-Sayed on "Face the Nation" about Jewish Michiganders' concerns regarding his ties to Piker, the far-left streamer who has appeared with him on the campaign trail. "There are Jewish voters in your state who are concerned about your relationship with Piker. You have condemned antisemitism but not called out his rhetoric directly. Why not?" Jiang asked. JEWISH DEM DEFECTIONS THREATEN EL-SAYED IN MICHIGAN SENATE RACE DECIDED BY RAZOR-THIN MARGINS Rather than answering the question, El-Sayed deflected, saying that voters were not asking him about Piker and that they were more focused on the issues impacting their daily lives. "Weiija, with all due respect, this is the third time you’ve asked about a Twitch streamer in California. I’ve done four events in Michigan this week. You know what didn’t come up? Twitch streamers in California," El-Sayed responded. The candidate said that voters would rather discuss grocery prices, healthcare and the environment, among other things. "I’m not interested in having a conversation about streamers in California because they are not raising the prices of gas and groceries," El-Sayed added. El-Sayed is not the first Democrat to push back on questions about Piker. Last month, Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., demanded reporters stop asking her about Piker, saying that "Republicans are trying to make" the race about him. EL-SAYED TORCHED ONLINE AFTER BRUSHING OFF QUESTIONS ABOUT HASAN PIKER CAMPAIGN TIES: ‘WHAT A PAL’ "I don’t agree with Hasan Piker on a lot of stuff, and I really don’t agree with him on some of the woman things he said. And I’m still trying to figure out, is it the reason he exercises and looks buff is why he has so many followers," Dingell said during a student town hall with El-Sayed and Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md. Piker has been vocal about his support for El-Sayed, going so far as to call on Democrats to punish those within the party who oppose the Michigan candidate. "You can't be out here saying like, 'Oh, I'm a centrist Democrat. And I think Abdul is a bridge too far.' That must be punished," Piker said during a stream in August. While El-Sayed previously appeared with Piker on the campaign trail, he told Semafor in August that he had "no plans" to campaign with the controversial streamer. This came after Piker, who is known for his inflammatory rhetoric and anti-Israel stance, made a remark about Jewish Americans' support for Israel that drew the ire of several Democrats. "People don't f--- with Israel any longer. And if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they're singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone will come around and take action not against Israel, mind you, but against American Jews," Piker said during his stream on Aug. 20. Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., condemned Piker in a statement, calling him "a hack who thrives on hate, shock and awe because he lacks substance." ABDUL EL-SAYED PLAYS DOWN HASAN PIKER TIES AFTER STREAMER’S VIRAL ANTISEMITISM FIRESTORM CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Several other Democratic lawmakers spoke out against Piker after he made the remarks, including Sens. Cory Booker, D-N.J.; Jon Ossoff, D-Ga.; Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich.; and Jacky Rosen, D-Nev.; House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.; and Reps. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J.; Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y.; Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla.; Brad Schneider, D-Ill.; and Greg Stanton, D-Ariz. El-Sayed also responded to Piker's comments, and while he did not condemn the streamer outright, he denounced antisemitism and rhetoric that puts the Jewish community in danger. "I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past," El-Sayed wrote at the time. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters," he added. "Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk."

articles.title: A Los Angeles home hosted 173 productions since 2021 and earned more than $1.5 million; now the 4,675-sq-ft property and its filming business are for sale for $3.245 million
articles.summary: News News: A Los Angeles home that has hosted 173 commercial productions since 2021 has been listed for $3.245 million, along with the filming business built aro.
articles.body: A Los Angeles home that has hosted 173 commercial productions since 2021 has been listed for $3.245 million, along with the filming business built around the property. The Woodland Hills residence, known as the Rum Punch House, has earned more than $1.5 million from filming and typically hosts productions for only 25 to 40 days a year.The five-bedroom, four-bathroom property has been used by major companies including Apple, Google, Microsoft, Walmart, Target, T-Mobile, Verizon, Instagram and Lowe's. Acccording to Realtor, the home's filming activity has generated an average of about $258,000 a year.The property at 6101 Shoup Ave. covers about 4,675 square feet and sits behind gates on a nearly 28,000-square-foot lot, or around 0.65 acre. The sale is being represented by Renee Leflore of Douglas Elliman and includes not just the house, but also the infrastructure and business connected to its use as a filming location.The home was completely redesigned in 2019 by its owners, photographer and commercial director Rob Deutschman and his wife, stylist Sybile Kohn-Deutschman. The couple had already spent more than three decades working in the production industry before turning their own home into a location for shoots.How the home became a filming locationDeutschman said his experience in the industry helped the couple understand what production teams look for when choosing a location."Sybile and I have been involved in various aspects of production for 30-plus years," Rob tells Realtor. "I as a fashion and advertising photographer and commercial director, and when I met Sybile, she was a wardrobe stylist."The couple later worked together as a creative team and travelled around the world for shoots involving major brands. That experience gave them an understanding of the practical requirements of commercial productions."It's much more than just the house," he explains. "It's the right neighborhood, parking for production, a very secluded and private property. This house checked all those boxes."When they redesigned the property, however, the couple did not create it only for production companies. They also wanted it to remain their home."We were able to go in and add all the things that we love and make it our home," he says. "Turns out what we love, so does the world of advertising."The redesign gave different parts of the house different looks and moods. This allows production teams to create different settings without having to move to another property.The interiors feature exposed wooden beams, handcrafted furnishings, artisan tile and a Caribbean-inspired colour palette. Sybile's design choices were influenced by her connection with the Caribbean, while Rob had also spent part of his career shooting fashion on islands."Sybile grew up in too many places to list, but the Caribbean had a major impact on her style choices," Rob explains. "Color and island comfort are her go-to. I spent a good part of my career on islands shooting fashion. We carried that aesthetic into the design of the property."Designed to change for different shootsThe owners also made sure the interiors could be changed depending on what a production required. "We intentionally created a space that can be used in many different ways," he says. "Leave it as is- tropical. Change out the interior, and it can be middle America.""The main thing about the house is it has great light and architecture," he adds. "As a commercial director, to me, it is a dream."The property has hosted everything from smaller setups to larger commercial campaigns. Deutschman said he generally does not discuss which brands or projects have used the house."In this industry, it is best not to talk about who, how often, and what was shot at the property," he says. "Having said that, there is one that stands out."One commercial was made for a car company and featured a couple who brought a stray sheep home as a pet. The animal was shown being treated like a dog, including being taken for a walk and given a bath, before causing damage around the house."Like a dog, they take it for a walk, give it a bath, it drinks from the toilet, and while they are gone, the sheep tears up the entire house," Rob recalls. "It was just great."The production used the home's Italian stone bathtub. "Having a sheep in our Italian stone bathtub getting a bubble bath was interesting," he says. "All went perfectly."What the $3.245 million sale includesAway from filming, the property has several features for everyday use. A swimming pool is surrounded by landscaped gardens, while other spaces include a meditation room, an art studio and a woodworking workshop.An upstairs retreat has a bedroom, loft and kitchenette. The space can be used by guests, extended family or as a workspace.The primary suite has direct access to a private zen garden. Its spa-style bathroom includes custom tilework and a brass rain showerhead. The kitchen has a professional-grade Viking range, a built-in four-door refrigerator and custom cabinetry. The property also has Sonos audio and a security camera system.Its location facilities have also been designed with production crews in mind. Neighbouring properties have historically provided parking for more than 80 crew vehicles, while crews can enter the yard through a rear gate.The sale also includes the established filming operation. This covers a database with more than 900 industry contacts, an existing website, professional photography and relationships built within the location industry.The Rum Punch House is represented by major location agencies and has received repeat business and referrals during its years as a filming destination.Owners see room for more filming workDeutschman believes a future owner could expand the business because the property has not been opened to every type of production."The potential is there," he says. "We limited our choices of projects and left out a part of the market such as feature films, reality shows, TV series, and music videos."He said these categories could provide another source of filming revenue. "These categories generate a lot of potential income," he says. "For us, we found the balance in sticking mainly to commercials and print advertising."According to information provided about the property, filming does not involve overnight stays and shoots generally finish by early to mid-evening. This has allowed the owners to continue living at the property while operating the filming business.The property has operated under the Rum Punch House name for six years since its redesign. It also has its own website and social media presence.For Leflore, the combination of a private Los Angeles home and an established production business is what makes the property unusual."The Rum Punch House in Woodland Hills is a remarkably desirable house because it perfectly bridges the gap between a luxurious compound and a highly lucrative income-generating production ecosystem," she says.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle pull Archie and Lilibet out of UK school after just two days over security concerns; Sussex children to move to another school after family's return to Britain
articles.summary: UK News: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have withdrawn their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, from their new school in Britain after just two days.
articles.body: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have withdrawn their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, from their new school in Britain after just two days, with the decision reportedly linked to security concerns surrounding the school run.Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, started at the prep school shortly after the Sussex family returned to Britain following six years in the United States. They are now expected to join another school in the area.A spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex confirmed that the decision followed discussions with the family's security team.“The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family’s security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements,” the spokesperson told HELLO! Magazine.“The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family. This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there.”Security concerns over school runAccording to the report, there was no problem with the school itself. Instead, concerns reportedly emerged over the practicalities of getting Archie and Lilibet safely to and from school.Security personnel had carried out checks on the school during the summer holidays after Harry and Meghan decided to return to Britain. However, the family's security team was reportedly unable to properly assess the school run until the start of term.Heavy traffic around the school is said to have made it difficult for the Sussex security convoy to remain together.A friend of the couple told the magazine that Harry and Meghan had wanted to make the arrangement work because their children had enjoyed the school.“It’s a real shame, because they absolutely adored the school, the kids and their parents. It was perfect for them in every way and the children really enjoyed their time there,” the friend said.“They really wanted to make it work, but they had to make a difficult decision based on the fact that the team couldn’t make the school run operationally secure.”Archie and Lilibet set to start at another schoolThe children are expected to attend another school in the area. According to the report, Archie and Lilibet visited the new school for a taster session on Monday.Prince Harry was reportedly seen settling Lilibet into reception, while Harry and Meghan have also been added to the school's parents' WhatsApp groups.The abrupt change comes only days after the children began their first school in Britain following the family's return.Meghan and Harry's security reviewThe school move comes as Meghan and Harry's security arrangements in Britain are again under review.Meghan has reportedly been granted her first government-backed security review since the couple stepped back from royal duties in 2020. Harry and Meghan have been asked to provide details of their daily routines, including the school run, as part of an assessment of any changes to the threat they face.Harry has been fighting to have his police protection reinstated since 2021. He pursued a legal challenge over the decision to remove his taxpayer-funded security, ultimately losing his Court of Appeal case in May 2025.During the legal battle, Harry said he could not see a situation in which he would bring his wife and children back to the UK because of his security concerns.The issue came back into focus during the family's UK visit in June, when Meghan withdrew from planned public appearances alongside Harry, with their team citing security concerns.In August, Harry and Meghan announced plans to move back to Britain with their children for an extended period, with Archie and Lilibet subsequently enrolled at a school in the area where the family is now living.Meghan gives glimpse into family's new lifeThe school decision comes a day after Meghan shared a series of photographs on Instagram offering a rare glimpse into the family's life in Britain.The pictures showed Harry, Meghan and their children enjoying outdoor activities, including fishing and woodland walks. Archie and Lilibet were also pictured wearing raincoats and Wellington boots.Prince Harry is due to make several public appearances in the coming days, although it has not been confirmed whether Meghan will accompany him.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: British Crown symbol was branded on enslaved Africans, research finds
articles.summary: The findings are part of a project documenting British involvement in the slave trade between the 16th and 19th Centuries.
articles.body:
Enslaved African people were branded with an identifying mark that included an emblem of the British Crown, according to new research by a project documenting British involvement in the slave trade.

Prof William Pettigrew, who led the Register of British Slave Traders research, described the imprinting as a "dramatic and harrowing" symbol of the monarchy's relationship to slavery.

The register lists 13,000 individuals and hundreds of institutions known to have invested in Britain's role in slavery between 1563 and 1807, when the trade was abolished across the British Empire.

Researchers say it is the most comprehensive examination of a national community of slave traders ever undertaken.

Dr Nicholas Radburn, historian at Lancaster University and co-investigator in the project, told the BBC he first found the identifying mark - which is an image of the Crown, with the South Sea Company logo below it - while looking through the company's archives at the British Library in 2022.

Founded in 1711, the South Sea Company was set up as a public and private British company and trafficked thousands of enslaved Africans.

Radburn said it was "remarkable" to find records of the branding "buried in a very nondescript sounding volume: 'The Register of Instruments'".

In 2024, he found letters that helped piece the story together. They were from the company's director to their "factors" (slave traders) in the Spanish Americas, Radburn explained.

"The letters were full of very detailed instructions on how to conduct the slave trade," he recalled.

One letter from February 1714 was "exceptional because it laid bare so clearly the ways in which the London-based directors were personally involved in the violence that was committed against the enslaved in the Americas".

The directors sent irons made in England for slave traders to use to mark enslaved African people on their left shoulder with the emblem.

The purpose, the letter outlined, was to distinguish the company's slaves from others.

In an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Pettigrew - from King's College London - said there were all sorts of connections between the monarchy and slavery, not just this "brutal imprint".

"If you think about the history of the monarchy when it was at its absolute lowest ebb, when King Charles I was executed, members of the royal family relaunched the monarchy, its finances and its reputation, by investing in the transatlantic slave trade," he said.

He said it was important to draw a distinction between the monarchy as an institution, and the individuals who led it.

"The institution is the same as it was hundreds of years ago.

"So when we talk about the role of the slave trade in rehabilitating the monarchy or improving its position, we're talking about an institution that is still very much a part of British life today.

"In a court of law, the monarchy is the same institution today as it was in the 17th Century."

In a statement, Buckingham Palace said King Charles "has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today".

The King is "grateful to all those undertaking academic work in this area and thus contributing to the debate about how such issues might best be addressed".

'The gravest crime against humanity': What does the UN vote on slavery mean?

The researchers say the register lays bare the breadth of which individuals contributed financially to the slave trade - from monarchs and politicians, to plumbers and clergymen.

"They financed wars, shaped modern industry, and built ports, canals and thriving cities, helping make Britain a global and imperial force," Pettigrew said.

Anyone who contributed financially to the transatlantic slave trade, or to a company enabling the trade, is listed in the database.

The register is a culmination of five years of research by Pettigrew and his team. It aims to highlight how individuals "financed the English (then British) contribution to the transatlantic traffic in enslaved African people".

The financing contributed to England's role in enslaving around three million African men, women and children, of whom an estimated half a million died during forced transportation, King's College London said.

African and Caribbean countries have called for a formal apology and reparations from countries that benefited from the transatlantic slave trade.

Earlier in September, Jamaica's government said it would raise a petition on the subject of slavery reparations with to King Charles, the country's head of state.

Olivia Grange, the country's culture minister, said the petition would ask the King to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council over the legality of the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica.

She said she hoped it would pave the way for a "long outstanding settlement for the hundreds of years of the most horrific abuse that our African ancestors endured".

Last week, a Downing Street spokesperson said the transatlantic slave trade was "abhorrent" but the UK position was that it does not pay reparations.

Finding Britain's Slave Traders with David Olusoga

articles.title: SC faults Abu Salem's maths, junks release plea
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court has ruled that if a person is convicted in two cases and sentenced separately, the period of imprisonment undergone as an und.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court has ruled that if a person is convicted in two cases and sentenced separately, the period of imprisonment undergone as an undertrial can be offset against only one of the sentences and not both even when the trial court had ordered the two sentences to run concurrently.The ruling was given by a bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta while detecting that gangster Abu Salem, who was extradited from Portugal in Nov 2005 on a solemn assurance by Indian govt that he would not be awarded death penalty or a jail term of more than 25 years, had computed his undertrial incarceration period twice to seek release from jail on the ground that he has already spent 25 years in jail, even though he was awarded life sentences in two terror cases in 2015 and 2017.Justice Nath said, "The fact that sentences imposed in the two cases were directed to run concurrently is of significance. Sentences granted concurrently operate simultaneously, hence the same period of incarceration cannot be notionally counted twice for the purpose of determining completion of the sentence.""The appellant (Salem) cannot treat the period preceding the later conviction as undertrial custody for one sentence while simultaneously treating the same period, from the date of the earlier conviction, as post-conviction custody for the other sentence and thereby secure a double benefit," Justice Nath said.SC said the sovereign commitment given to Portugal govt that no sentence extending beyond 25 years would be imposed upon Salem has no bearing on the judicial determination of Salem's guilt in two terror cases and award of life sentences."Prescription of the nature and extent of punishment is governed by the Legislature and its application to the facts of a particular case falls within the domain of the Judiciary. The Executive, in turn, exercises such powers in relation to remission, commutation or release as are conferred upon it by law," it said.SC referred to the govt affidavit which had categorised Salem among prisoners who have been sentenced to 50 years of imprisonment. After reducing the set-off and remission periods, it had informed SC that the probable date of Salem's release would be Jan 31, 2046, that is, after another 20 years.Dismissing Salem's appeal, SC said the calculations carried out by govt indicate that he continues to serve life sentence and "the stipulation that he cannot be detained beyond 25 years is a consequence of the sovereign assurance extended by Union govt to Portugal's govt. It does not convert sentence of life imprisonment into a fixed-term sentence of 25 years".Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Landowners in Texas ask court to stop Trump border wall
articles.summary: Indigenous groups, environmentalists and locals oppose the wall; Big Bend sees about 1 percent of border arrests.
articles.body:
A group of landowners, ranchers, businesses and a non-profit organisation have sued the administration of United States President Donald Trump to stop construction of a wall along the country’s border with Mexico in the remote Big Bend region of the southern state of Texas.

Trump officials “were woefully unprepared for the hornet’s nest they stirred up because they had no idea how much we love this place”, David Keller, an archaeologist and historian who specialises in the Big Bend and lives in the region, said in a news conference announcing the lawsuit on Monday.

“For us, the Big Bend is not an empty place on the map,” he said. “It is our home.”

The lawsuit was filed by Conserve Big Bend and six landowners, with the support of dozens more people along the border.

It comes as the Trump administration is ramping up a $46bn effort to line the roughly 3,219km (2,000-mile) border with a collection of 9-metre (30-foot) steel bollard walls, vehicle barriers and technology intended to keep out smugglers and migrants.

In Arizona, federal officials are pushing ahead with construction of the border infrastructure, even though it cuts through land belonging to the Tohono O’odham Nation, an Indigenous tribe that has said it does not want the barrier and that it is unnecessary.

In Texas, the effort has run up against numerous lawsuits and bipartisan opposition from sheriffs, elected officials, tour guides, environmental groups and landowners.

As part of its wall-building efforts, the administration has waived numerous regulations and statutes designed to protect the environment, archaeology or wildlife, on the basis that there is an urgent need to protect the border in what the US Department of Homeland Security has called areas of “high illegal entry”.

But in the lawsuit announced on Monday, the plaintiffs argue that when it comes to the Big Bend region, that is not an accurate description. They cite historical statistics from US Customs and Border Protection showing how few people cross the border in Big Bend compared with other areas along the US-Mexico border.

Big Bend has about 805km (500 miles) of border, roughly one quarter of the total length of the border with Mexico from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico. But the region accounted for only about 1 percent of arrests, according to the lawsuit.

articles.title: Free diver spots jellyfish the 'size of a bus' near Pembrokeshire coastline
articles.summary: Iestyn Morgan has set out to make Welsh aquatic life "more accessible" for people to see.
articles.body:
A free diver has said he "couldn't believe his luck" after spotting a giant jellyfish off the Welsh coastline.

Iestyn Morgan, from Pembrokeshire, said the lion's mane was the "length of a bus" with a size of about 10 to 15 metres (32ft 8in to 49ft 2in).

The 21-year-old conservationist, who records footage for social media to raise awareness about the "threats our seas are facing" , said it was the first lion's mane he had seen in Wales.

More commonly found in the colder waters off Scotland, a marine biologist said although the lion's main sting was "nasty", it was not dangerous.

Morgan said he was swimming near Trefin Beach in Pembrokeshire when he spotted the tentacles in the water.

"Three turned to 10, and then to 20. They just kept on coming," he added.

The jellyfish was so big the tentacles went "beyond the range of visibility".

He initially thought it was a compass jellyfish , which are native to UK waters, before realising it was too big.

"It must have been the length of a bus or small train. I couldn't believe how big it was."

The Wildlife Trusts said the lion's mane jellyfish gets its name from its long tentacles, and have "all the beauty and bite of a lion".

They can grow up to 3m (9ft 8in) in length, but the tentacles - which are used to catch their prey - can exceed 30 to 36.5 metres (98ft 4in to 119ft 8in) making it one of the longest animals on Earth.

Marine biologist Dr Cathy Lucas, from the University of Southampton, said Morgan's video showed the animal's incredible length.

"The tentacles are so long and so fine you might not even see them," she said, recalling how during field work in Scotland divers would get bits of tentacles on them when there were no jellyfish around.

"They still sting after they break off," she said, adding that while the sting was "nasty" and "the worst in the UK", it was not dangerous.

"The advice is not to touch them and if you get a bit of tentacle on your skin flick it off with a stick and wash in warm water to neutralise," she said.

Lucas said lion's manes "occasionally" reach the Welsh coast later in the summer or autumn, according to jellyfish sightings recorded by the public, but their main habitat in the UK was Scotland.

Morgan feels we should be "grateful" they were in Wales, adding they were not "big scary monsters" as some people may think.

"Your biggest problem is if you swim into them. You don't want to get stung by a lion's mane."

Morgan said he was seeing "more and more" jellyfish coming into Welsh waters as he was filming.

He said it was part of a theme in which he was noticing warm water species "becoming more abundant".

"I don't have enough summers to compare it to, but I put down a camera a few weeks ago and saw a Triggerfish, which is native to the Mediterranean," he added.

Morgan said creating his content has been "very rewarding" as he wanted to make aquatic environments "more accessible" to people.

But he was always conscious that he never wanted to harm the animals as part of his project.

"I don't want to turn it into something that I'm going out to hunt the animals or anything," he said.

"I just get in the water, film and swim."

articles.body: Braden “Clavicular” Peters was kicked out of the Church of Scientology in Los Angeles after a tense moment during his recent Kick livestream, Touring Around Hollywood. The streamer was seen loudly calling for help inside the building and repeatedly claiming that people were trying to kill him. After he was removed, Clavicular stayed outside and spoke to people near the church, warning them against entering and repeatedly telling them to “seek Jesus Christ.” A clip of the incident was later shared on X by @FearedBuck. Sportskeeda reported on the incident, while the Church of Scientology’s official website confirms the Los Angeles church is on Sunset Boulevard.Braden “Clavicular” Peters repeatedly calls for help inside churchThe situation became heated when Clavicular began shouting inside the Church of Scientology. He repeatedly claimed that someone was trying to kill him and asked people around him for help. The streamer made the same claims several times before staff and security removed him from the building.In the clip shared on X, Clavicular can be heard saying:“Oh, s**t. He’s trying to kill me! They’re trying to kill me! They’re trying to kill me! Help! They’re trying to kill me! He said he’s gonna kill me! They’re trying to kill me! He said he’s gonna kill me! He said he’s gonna kill me! Help, help, help, help, help, help, help, help, help! They’re trying to kill me. They’re trying to kill me. Guys, they’re trying to kill me! Help! Help!”He was then kicked out of the church. The Church of Scientology’s official site lists its Los Angeles location at 4810 Sunset Boulevard and says the building has been serving the city from the site since 1977.Braden “Clavicular” Peters tells people they need Jesus ChristBeing removed from the building did not end the confrontation. Clavicular continued talking to people outside and told them not to go into the church. He also made several negative comments about the organization before repeatedly turning his message toward Christianity.He told people that they needed God and Jesus Christ, repeating the message several times:“You need God. Look, you need Jesus. You need Jesus. You need Jesus. You need Jesus. I’m hugging you. You need Jesus. You need Jesus.”The incident was part of Clavicular’s Touring Around Hollywood livestream and quickly became the main focus of the clip shared from the broadcast. The Church of Scientology has not publicly commented on the reported confrontation in the sources reviewed for this article.The Los Angeles church describes itself as a place where visitors can learn about Scientology and offers public tours. articles.title: Abbott agrees to pay nearly $385 million to US government over alleged false claims tied to infant formula made at Michigan facility; contamination allegations, company history and settlement explained
articles.summary: US News: Abbott Laboratories, the Illinois-based healthcare company that manufactures and sells infant formula and nutritional therapy products, has agreed to .
articles.body: Abbott Laboratories, the Illinois-based healthcare company that manufactures and sells infant formula and nutritional therapy products, has agreed to pay $384,999,040 to resolve allegations that it caused false claims to be submitted to federal and state programs.The allegations relate to the company's failure to manufacture certain powdered infant formula and nutritional therapy products at its facilities in Sturgis, Michigan, and Casa Grande, Arizona, in compliance with federal and state statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements between January 1, 2018, and December 31, 2022.The settlement was announced by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Michigan.Allegations involved WIC and Medicaid programsThe U.S. Department of Agriculture funds and regulates the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), which provides nutritional assistance, including infant formula, to eligible participants.More than half of all infant formula purchased in the United States is paid for through USDA funds via WIC. State Medicaid programs also cover and pay for certain infant formula products.According to a complaint filed by the United States in November 2025, Abbott allegedly caused WIC programs to purchase powdered infant formula manufactured at its Sturgis facility despite the products allegedly failing to meet statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements.The complaint alleged that Abbott knowingly manufactured infant formula purchased with taxpayer money in conditions that created an unacceptable risk of microorganism contamination.Government alleges manufacturing and contamination concernsThe complaint further alleged that Abbott failed to properly maintain manufacturing equipment and failed to control the presence of water that could encourage microorganism growth.It also alleged that the company fostered a culture of concealment that failed to systematically identify, document, investigate and prevent potential contamination.“When someone supplies the government with food that is meant to be given to our infant children, we demand that it meet or exceed every federal nutrition and safety requirement,” U.S. Attorney Timothy VerHey said.“This case demonstrates that anyone who fails this standard will pay a high price.”Abbott to pay nearly $349 million to USUnder the civil settlement agreement, Abbott will pay $348,700,868 to the United States to resolve the False Claims Act allegations.The company will also pay $36,298,172 to certain states for claims settled by their state Medicaid and WIC programs.The settlement resolves claims brought under the False Claims Act's qui tam provisions, which allow private individuals to file lawsuits on behalf of the US government concerning alleged false claims submitted to federal programs and potentially share in any recovery.The underlying lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan under the caption United States, et al. ex rel. Scott Millard, et al. v. Abbott Laboratories, No. 1:22-cv-994.Justice Department and USDA investigatedThe resolution resulted from a coordinated effort involving the Justice Department's Civil Division, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Michigan and the USDA's Office of Inspector General.The Justice Department said its Civil Division's False Claims Act enforcement is intended to combat alleged fraud involving federal programs and recover money for taxpayers.The matter was handled by Civil Fraud Section Trial Attorneys Asha Natarajan and Erin Colleran of the Justice Department's Civil Division, along with Assistant U.S. Attorneys Whitney Schnurr and Jacob Carlton of the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Michigan.Allegations do not establish liabilityThe government stressed that the claims resolved through the settlement are allegations only and that there has been no determination of liability.The settlement therefore resolves the government's allegations without a finding that Abbott was liable for the claims described in the complaint.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: I got paid $5,000 to move to a place I'd never heard of
articles.summary: Relocation schemes offer support for people who want to swap big cities for a cheaper, quieter life.
articles.body:
When Brianna Beyrouti looks back on her former life in the city of Portland, Oregon, she says she had been financially "drowning".

"I was absolutely living paycheque to paycheque. Every time the smallest thing came up, it was like 'Oh, gosh, the kids need shoes, how am I going to afford that?' As a single parent, everything falls on my shoulders."

Last year, Brianna left Portland and its metropolitan population of 2.5 million people.

She and her two children moved 2,000 miles east to Muncie, Indiana, a small city with 65,000 people, a university and lots of open space, taking advantage of a scheme that contributed $5,000 towards the cost of the move to boost population growth.

The relocation has been a revelation for her finances. She continues to work remotely for the same bank, so her annual salary of $107,000 (£79,000) is unchanged, but she has been able to buy a home for the first time. And her mortgage is less than she used to have to pay in rent.

In Portland she was paying rent of $1,290 a month for an apartment, while the combined cost of her mortgage, home insurance and property tax for her detached home in Muncie is $1,100.

Add the fact that state income tax is lower in Indiana, and that her car insurance and energy bills have also fallen, and Brianna says she is $600 a month better off.

"I'm able to live my life more than I was before," she says. "When my kids want something, I'm much more inclined to say yes. My quality of life has increased dramatically."

Brianna is not alone in swapping a big city for a smaller one.

As the high cost of living continues to bite in the US, many of the biggest cities are seeing their populations fall, as people leave in search of cheaper property.

A 2025 report from the National Association of Realtors found that for people moving to a different state, affordability was their primary reason.

As a result, big cities from the likes of New York and Los Angeles to Portland, Oregon have seen a dip in their populations in recent years, further fuelled by the greatly increased acceptance of remote working since the Covid-19 pandemic.

By contrast, some small towns and cities across the US, such as Muncie, are seeing their populations rise after decades of decline. The number of people who live in Muncie hit 65,466 last year, official figures showed. This is up from 65,194 in 2020, but still way down on its population of 71,828 in 1990.

To help it stand out from the crowd, and encourage remote workers to move there from outside Indiana, Muncie's local council offers them $5,000 in cash to cover their relocation costs.

It does this via a website called MakeMyMove, which lists several such relocation support schemes offered by similar small cities and towns across the US. These pay MakeMyMove a subscription fee.

Other incentives locations offer potential new residents are complementary cinema tickets, restaurant vouchers, and even free bottles of wine.

Brianna and her children are one of around 100 families to have moved to Muncie through the MakeMyMove programme. She says she hadn't heard of the city before.

Across the US, MakeMyMove says it helped 1,000 people in total relocate last year, and is on target to increase that to 1,500 in 2026.

Scientist Elena Chrysostomou also used a relocation support scheme to swap a big city for smalltown US. In 2024 she relocated from San Diego, California, to Jacksonville, a town of 17,700 people in rural Illinois.

The move was backed by the Jacksonville Regional Economic Development Corporation (JREDC), which gave her $5,000 in cash, plus a "quality of life package" worth $4,000 that includes free gym memberships and golf passes.

The JREDC says that while the region is "already a great place to live", the support scheme helps to "sweeten the deal".

Elena was spending $3,000 renting a one-bedroom apartment in San Diego, but she now owns a three-bedroom home, with a mortgage of $1,868. At the same time, her salary has gone up 22% after she changed jobs, and her commute has gone down from a 15-minute drive to one of just one minute.

"I never thought that I'd be able to afford a house on my own, I always thought I'd need a partner, and even then, in San Diego, it would be so tough," she says.

"It's just more freeing. There's more security and independence."

While both she and Brianna have no regrets, they do admit to some drawbacks to their new lives. These include the narrower range of activities and restaurant choices, leaving behind friends and family, and for Brianna the difficulty of settling her children into new schools.

And while in Portland Brianna enjoyed walking to parks and shops, she now relies on her car to get anywhere.

But overall she says she is thrilled. "I have the biggest savings I've ever had in my life, and I'm a homeowner, and I can do things with my kids – we actually went on vacation for the first time in my youngest's life."
